findings: The 10-month average rule on 156 years of the S&P 500, acting a month late so monthly averaging cannot flatter it: Sharpe 0.64 against 0.56 for holding, worst drawdown -48% against -77%; the Sharpe gain's 90% range is -0.05 to +0.21. Of all 22 lengths the best is 12 months; judged on return alone, a no-edge world produces one that good 99.6% of the time: the rule cuts risk, not the return.
CAPE 40.9 is above 99% of months since 1881; history implies 0.4% a year real for ten years (80% range -5.6% to 5.9%). Over one year valuation explains almost nothing.

Markov-switching: a calm regime (10% annual volatility) lasting about 33 months and a turbulent one (29%) lasting about 7; today's chance of the turbulent regime is 2% (a two-state model on stocks since 1871; the decision and portfolio engines use richer models and put the stressed state higher).
Of 34 indicator and calendar tests, 15 pass at 5% before correction, 12 after controlling the false discovery rate, 8 after Holm.
